senses.definition: One of a series of berths or beds placed in tiers.
examples: Jane sleeps in the top bunk, and her little sister Lauren takes the bottom bunk.

quotes.text: The men resided in a huge bunk house, which consisted of one room only, with a shack outside where the cooking was done. In the large room were a dozen bunks ; half of them in a very dishevelled state, […]
quotes.reference: 1913, Robert Barr, chapter 6, in Lord Stranleigh Abroad:

senses.definition: (nautical) A built-in bed on board ship, often erected in tiers one above the other.
(informal) A bed in a prison, worksite or similar location.
(US) A wooden case or box, which serves for a seat in the daytime and for a bed at night.
(US, dialect) A piece of wood placed on a lumberman's sled to sustain the end of heavy timbers.
(Singapore, military, by extension) A dormitory or bunkroom where soldiers sleep.

examples: Due to bed shortages, Jeff and Paul had to bunk together.
What she said about me was total bunk. Don't believe a word.

quotes.text: “You can’t pull any bunk like that on us!” roared Quelch. “We’ve had enough of this flapdoodlery! Take your money, Mrs. Clinton, and sign the deed.”
quotes.reference: 1927, Arthur Train, When Tutt Meets Tutt, New York: Charles Scribner's Sons, page 47:

senses.definition: (obsolete) In early use often in the form the bunk.

quotes.text: This knife-throwing act is the bunk

senses.definition: (slang) A specimen of a recreational drug with insufficient active ingredient.

quotes.text: I still can get off with a pound of bunk and pretend it's some Runtz
quotes.reference: 2020 July 18, Rio Da Yung OG, featured by T LB$, “Toledo 2 Flint”, in The World is Yours, 1:26–1:28:

senses.definition: (British, India, slang) To fail to attend school or work without permission; to play truant (usually 'to bunk off').
examples: The naughty boys decided to bunk school and visit the comic shop.

senses.definition: (UK, dated, slang) To expel from a school.

quotes.text: She was bunked from the convent last term. I don't quite know what for.
quotes.reference: 1945, Evelyn Waugh, chapter 4, in Brideshead Revisited […], London: Chapman & Hall, published 1952, →OCLC, book 1 (Et in Arcadia Ego), pages 83–84:

quotes.text: "They're moving off," he said. "[…] [T]he funny little man with the beard like a goat is going a different way from everyone else — the gardeners will have to head him off. I don't see Mademoiselle, though. The rest of you had better bunk. […]"

You may well say chance it, lad. From what I see and what I hear it seems to be getting a pretty near thing which side touches down first, but the old geezer's dead set on going through whatever turns up, and God knows that if it comes to a general bunk he's bound to be the hindmost.
